doc.title: Sheila Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Middleburgh, New York, May 11, 2002

title: Detroit police stop her for mixing with black musicians
summary: She recounts being stopped and taken in by Detroit police while riding with Frank Foster and friends, and a cop's threat.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Oh it was horrible. They would stop us in the car, if they’d see you mixing they used to call it. Mix. They didn’t want you to mix as they say, you know, the blacks with the whites. And they’d see you in a car, the cops would stop. “Where were you born? Where are you going? Where are you coming from?” I mean third degree like you wouldn’t believe. I’ve been taken down to the police station in Detroit when I was going with Frank Foster. We were going out to Belle Isle, Frank Foster and myself were in the back and my girlfriend and the guy she was going with, they were sitting in the front. And we were both white and they were black you know, or Afro-American. These cops, plainclothesmen, stopped us and gave us the third degree. And then I threw a cigarette out of the car, and of course they crawled under the car to get that cigarette because they thought I was smoking dope. And in those days if you got caught with marijuana, I would still be in jail in Detroit. I mean they — anything that they could get on me as a young white girl hanging out with black musicians, they were going to be on your case. I never went out with people for that reason. I went with them because I didn’t even know color. I’m one-quarter Cherokee Native American. So am I gonna? I mean I know that feeling growing up being called a half-breed and the whole trip, when I still lived in Pennsylvania with my grandparents as a kid. I knew that prejudice. So to walk into this prejudice was like so heavy. I mean I fought so hard to do this music, and that was one of the hardest battles, was to not have the fear to stick up to these people of authority knowing that I was right and they were wrong. And they were the problem, not me. But the last time I got busted, I call it, was Frank Foster in the car, they took us down, they separated the women from the guys. This cop said to me, and I’ll never forget it as long as I live, he said, “I’m going to tell you something.” He said, “I have a 9-year-old daughter,” he said, “if I caught my daughter the way I caught you tonight, if I thought that was going to happen to her I would take this gun and go home and blow her brains
